1.sense: The surah opens on a condition with no answer attached to it yet. Four when-clauses run before the sentence finishes, and the first of them takes the roof off. The verb describes a tear along a seam rather than a demolition from outside.

notes.t: The verb comes from f-t-r, the root behind iftar, the breaking of a fast, and fitrah, the original state a thing was made on. The picture is of something coming apart along the line it was made on.
The Qur'an describes the sky in its present condition as a guarded ceiling that a searching eye finds no rift in, which is what makes this splitting an event rather than a description.

A report from Ibn Umar has the Prophet ﷺ say that whoever wishes to look at the Day of Rising as though he were seeing it should recite At-Takwir, Al-Infitar and Al-Inshiqaq. It is carried in Tirmidhi and Ahmad and its grading is discussed.
notes.src: Tirmidhi, Book of Tafsir, from Ibn ʿUmar; graded hasan by some and weak by others

links.why: the same event opened with a different verb, the sky giving way to its Lord
the sky splitting and turning red like oiled leather

2.sense: The second clause. The verb is the one used for a string of beads breaking and the beads going everywhere at once. What is described is not stars burning out but stars losing the arrangement they were holding.

notes.t: Nathara is to scatter loose things by hand, seed thrown or beads off a broken thread. The related noun nathr is prose, speech that has not been strung into verse. The stars are being unstrung.
The Qur'an says the lowest sky was adorned with lamps, so the scattering undoes an arrangement that had been described as decoration.
The four opening clauses move downward in order: sky, stars, seas, graves. The last one is the only one the reader is personally inside.

links.why: the stars falling, in the surah that shares this scene
the stars obliterated when the sentence comes

3.sense: Fujjirat is the verb for opening a spring in rock or cutting a canal through a bank. Something held back is let out. The limits that keep the seas apart from each other and off the land are taken away and the waters run together.

notes.t: The same root gives fajr, daybreak, because dawn is light bursting through the edge of the night. The sense is release, not evaporation.
The Qur'an describes a barrier between two seas that neither one crosses. This verse is that barrier being removed.

The exegetes read the verb two ways here: the seas breaking their limits and running into one another, and the seas set alight, reading this verse alongside the line in At-Takwir about seas being kindled.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both senses; Ibn Kathir joins the verse to 81:6

links.why: the seas set alight in the parallel scene
the barrier between the two seas, in force until this day

4.sense: The fourth clause, and the one that concerns the reader directly. The verb is used of a container upended and its contents tipped out, and of ground dug up and turned over. The graves do not open. They are emptied.

notes.t: The Qur'an uses this same verb of the graves in Al-Adiyat and pairs it there with the contents of the chests being brought out, so an opened grave and an opened inner life arrive together.
All four openings use a passive verb and none of them names an agent. Nobody is said to be doing any of it until the last verse of the surah settles whose command that day is.
Three of the clauses describe places no living person can reach. The fourth describes the one place every living person is going.

links.why: the same verb of the graves, with the chests emptied alongside them
they come out of the graves hurrying toward their Lord

5.sense: The answer to the four conditions, and it is neither a punishment nor a reward. It is knowledge. After all that machinery comes apart, what happens is that a person finally knows the whole account of what they sent forward and what they left behind them.

notes.t: Nafsun is indefinite and singular, one soul, which in Arabic distributes across all of them. The grammar makes the reckoning individual rather than collective.
The verse does not say a soul will be told or shown. It says a soul will know, which removes the room a person would need to argue with the record.

Qaddamat and akhkharat are read several ways: deeds sent ahead against deeds postponed, the good done first against the good delayed, and what a person did against the practices they set running that kept working after their death.
notes.src: at-Tabari lists the readings; Ibn Kathir includes what a person leaves behind them

links.why: man is informed that Day of what he sent ahead and what he left
the Day each soul finds what it did placed in front of it

6.sense: The scene stops and a question is put straight to the reader. Not what made you deny, or what made you sin, but what fooled you. The last word of the question is the one that does the work: the Lord being taken lightly is named as the Generous.

notes.t: Gharra is to take somebody in, to leave them with a false sense of safety. The same root gives ghurur, the deceptive appeal the Qur'an attaches to worldly life. A man under ghurur is not defiant, he is comfortable.
The question is left unanswered in the surah. The exegetes noticed the gap and read it as deliberate, since the honest answer differs from one person to the next.

More than one early exegete read the naming of Allah as al-Karim inside the question as itself the answer: it was His own generosity, His covering of faults and His delay in punishing, that a man mistook for indifference.
notes.src: reported from several early exegetes; the commentaries carry the reading without agreeing to settle on it

links.why: the deceiver deceived you about Allah, said at the wall on that Day
do not let the great deceiver deceive you about Allah

7.sense: Three verbs in sequence, each joined by fa, which in Arabic means the next followed directly from the one before. Made, then evened out, then balanced. What your Lord did for you is given as a process you were carried through without noticing any of it.

notes.t: Sawwa is to make a thing level and proportioned, the verb for a builder finishing a wall. Adala is to put equal weight on both sides. Together they describe symmetry: two eyes at one height, two hands the same length, a body that stands up.
The Qur'an uses the second of these verbs of Adam, when He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit, so the sequence here describes every human being in the terms used of the first one.

The third verb is recited two ways among the canonical readings. Hafs, the reading of this Mushaf, has ʿadalaka with a single dal; other readers double it as ʿaddalaka, which strengthens the sense to made you perfectly even. Both are transmitted readings.
notes.src: the canonical readings differ here between ʿadalaka and ʿaddalaka

links.why: We created man in the best proportion
He formed you and made your forms good

8.sense: The form you have was chosen, and it was chosen out of others He could have chosen instead. Rakkaba is the verb for fitting parts together into a working whole, the word used for mounting a rider on an animal and for putting a structure together from its pieces.

notes.t: The verse concedes that your particular face and build are one option among many. It does not flatter the reader by calling the result the best available. It says the choosing was His.
The Qur'an says the same of the shaping of a person before birth, that He forms you in the wombs however He wills.
Set beside verse six, the argument runs like this: the One you were fooled about is the One who assembled the body you are currently using to be fooled in.

links.why: He shapes you in the wombs however He wills
He formed you, made your forms good, and provided for you

9.sense: The question is cut off before an excuse can be produced. Kalla refuses, and bal turns the sentence to the real matter. The address changes number at the same moment: the question in verse six was to one man, this is to a crowd.

notes.t: Din here carries the sense it has in Al-Fatiha's Master of the Day of Din, an account being settled rather than a religion. What is being named is the denial that anything is going to be added up.
Tukadhdhibuna is not the verb for doubting. It is the verb for calling a report a lie, which is something done to a speaker rather than a private uncertainty a person carries around.
The Qur'an makes the same move in Al-Maʿun, where denying the reckoning is put underneath a man's conduct rather than beside it as a separate opinion.

links.why: the same denial named, then shown by what a man does with an orphan
those who deny the Day of Recompense, described from the inside

10.sense: The denial is answered with a fact about the room rather than an argument. Whatever you make of the reckoning, there are keepers assigned to you, and the word alaykum places them above rather than alongside.

notes.t: Hafiz is the same word used of a person who has memorised the Qur'an and of a guard on a gate. It means one who holds a thing without letting any of it drop.

The Prophet ﷺ described angels of the night and angels of the day who take turns over people and meet at the dawn and the afternoon prayers, and said that Allah asks them, though He knows best, how they left His servants, and they answer that they left them praying and came to them while they were praying.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Abu Hurayra

notes.t: The sentence carries both inna and the emphatic lam, which is about the strongest ordinary way Arabic has of pressing a statement on someone. It is being pressed on people who assumed they were unobserved.

links.why: no word is uttered without a watcher ready beside the speaker
attendants before him and behind him, keeping him by the command of Allah

11.sense: Two words about the keepers. They are noble, and they write. The first rules out the picture of a hostile clerk waiting for a slip. The second settles what kind of record it is, written rather than remembered.

notes.t: Karim was the word given to the Lord five verses earlier. The same adjective is now given to the ones He set over people, which keeps the whole arrangement of a single character.
The Qur'an says the record will be produced and spread open, and that the man will be told to read it himself and to reckon his own account.
Writing is slower and more deliberate than watching. What this verse adds to the one before it is permanence.

links.why: read your record, your own soul is enough of an accountant against you
the record leaves out nothing small and nothing large

12.sense: The third statement about them and the shortest. They know. Not they see, which would leave room for something misread, and not they hear, which would leave room for something done quietly.

notes.t: The three verses build in order: they are set over you, they write, they know. Each one closes off a way of imagining that something got past.
Both verbs are in the present tense, they know what you do, which describes an arrangement running now rather than a report filed at death.

What Allah Himself knows is stated elsewhere in stronger terms, that He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the chests conceal. The keepers hold a record; they are not the source of the knowledge.

links.why: He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal
Allah has counted it up while they forgot it

13.sense: After the record comes the outcome, given in two flat lines with nothing between them. The good are in delight. There is no verb in the Arabic sentence at all, which states a settled condition rather than a future event.

notes.t: Abrar comes from birr, the wide word for goodness done to other people, the same word used of dutifulness to parents. It is not a term for private piety.
The Qur'an describes the abrar at length in Al-Insan and traces their delight back to feeding a poor man, an orphan and a captive on a day they wanted the food themselves.
Naʿim is left indefinite, a delight, unspecified. This surah never describes the garden. It only says which side of the line a person is on.

links.why: the same sentence about the abrar, in the surah that follows this one
the abrar named and the deed that put them there

14.sense: The mirror of the line before it, matched structure for structure. Fujjar are people who burst out of their limits, and the word comes from the same root as the seas bursting in verse three.

notes.t: Verse three used the verb of seas breaking the barrier that held them. This verse uses the noun of people who did the same with theirs. The surah showed you the picture before it used the word.
Jahim is one of the Qur'an's names for the fire and the root carries the sense of a fire made to burn harder. Like naʿim in the verse before, it is left indefinite rather than named as a known place.
The Qur'an sets these two words against each other again in Al-Mutaffifin, where the record of the fujjar is in Sijjin and the record of the abrar in ʿIlliyyun.

links.why: the record of the fujjar, named in the surah that follows
the Qur'an refusing to treat the God-fearing and the fujjar as one

15.sense: The word din comes back six verses after they were accused of denying it. The thing they called a lie is now given as the date of their entry.

notes.t: Sala is the verb for roasting a thing over a fire, in contact with it, not for standing near heat. The Arabic keeps the whole matter physical.
The pronoun at the end of the first word points back to the jahim of the previous verse, so the two verses run as one sentence and the fire is named before they reach it.
The Day named here is the one named in verse nine as the thing being denied, which makes this an answer rather than a new subject.

links.why: then they will burn in the blaze, said of the same group
those who swallow the property of orphans will burn in a blaze

16.sense: One added clause removes the last thing left to hope for in the picture, which is an interval. They are not absent from it. No time off, no being taken elsewhere and brought back.

notes.t: Ghaʾib is the ordinary word for a man who is away, out of town, not present at a gathering. The verse takes a domestic word and denies it.
The bi attached to ghaʾibin adds emphasis in Arabic. A flatter way of saying this existed and was not used.
Some exegetes read the verse as denying them any absence once they are inside it, and others as denying that the fire is ever out of their sight, including before they enter.
notes.src: at-Tabari and the later commentaries carry both senses without ruling between them

links.why: it is not lightened for them and they are left in despair inside it
neither finished off nor lightened for them

17.sense: The address turns back to a single listener and the question is put to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Whatever that Day is, it lies outside anything a person could work out from what he has already seen.

notes.t: The Qur'an uses this formula in a fixed way. Where it asks ma adraka, what could make you know, an answer follows. Where it asks ma yudrika, what will make you know, no answer follows and the matter is left with Allah.
The verb adra is causative, to be brought to knowledge by something. The question is not whether the listener is clever, it is whether anything in his experience could carry the information.
The same phrase introduces other named things in the short surahs, among them the Night of Decree and the crushing fire.

links.why: the same question asked of the Night of Decree, and then answered
the same formula, answered with a name rather than a description

18.sense: The question is asked a second time and nothing is added to it except thumma, then. In Arabic thumma puts distance between two things, so the repetition is not a stammer. It is the same question asked again from further away.

notes.t: The Qur'an rarely repeats an entire verse like this outside Ar-Rahman and Al-Mursalat, where the repeated line is a refrain running through a list. Here the repetition falls twice in a row on one question.
An answer does arrive in the next verse, but it does not describe the Day. It states one fact about it, which is that nobody can do anything for anybody.
The exegetes differ over what the repetition is doing: plain emphasis, or a second and heavier raising of the matter signalled by thumma.
notes.src: ar-Razi and others argue both; the commentaries do not settle on one

links.why: the same warning doubled with thumma, no indeed they will come to know
the same doubling used on a different warning

19.sense: The answer to the doubled question, and it is a single statement about ownership. No soul holds anything on behalf of another soul. Family, rank, money and patronage are all arrangements where one person holds something for another, and none of them is in force.

notes.t: Tamliku is the verb of owning and of having authority over. It is the root behind the title Master of the Day of Recompense in Al-Fatiha, so this verse says plainly what that title implied.

The Prophet ﷺ gathered his relatives and named them one by one, including his own daughter, telling each of them to ask him for what they wished of his wealth but that he could not avail them anything against Allah.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Abu Hurayra

notes.t: The Qur'an does not deny intercession outright. It denies unpermitted intercession, saying nobody intercedes with Him except by His leave, and the two statements stand together.

links.why: Master of the Day of Recompense, the title this verse spells out
who may intercede at all, and on what condition

1.sense: The surah opens with a command, and the object of the command is a name. Not glorify your Lord, but glorify the name of your Lord, which puts the instruction on something a tongue can actually carry out. The name given is a superlative, the Highest, and the Qur'an joins it to Rabb in only one other place.

notes.t: Sabbaha is not praise. It is the declaring that a thing is clear of every defect people attach to it. The root sense is moving freely through water, so the word carries the putting of distance between your Lord and what is said of Him.
The Prophet ﷺ used to recite this surah together with Al-Ghashiya in the Friday prayer and in the prayer of the two Eids.
notes.src: Muslim, Book of Jumuʿa, from an-Nuʿman ibn Bashir

notes.t: A report has it that when this verse came down the Prophet ﷺ said to put it in the prostration, which is where the words Subhana Rabbiya al-Aʿla come from. The chain of that report is criticised, though the wording said in prostration is established by continuous practice.
notes.src: Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah, from ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir; the chain is criticised and gradings differ

links.why: the only other place the Qur'an joins this name to Rabb
the matching command, glorify the name of your Lord the Great

2.sense: The reason for the command starts here and runs for four verses without a break. Created, then evened out. No object is attached to either verb, so this is not the creation of one named thing but creation as such.

notes.t: The same two verbs ran through the question put to man in Al-Infitar. There they described one body. Here nothing is named, so they cover everything made.
The fa between the two verbs means the second followed the first directly. Making and finishing are one act in two stages, not a rough attempt and then a repair.
The Qur'an uses the second verb of the sky as well as of the body, saying He turned to the heaven and proportioned it into seven.

links.why: the same two verbs used of a single human body
an oath by a soul and by the One who proportioned it

3.sense: The second pair. He set a measure for each thing and then showed it the way to what it was measured for. This is guidance in the widest sense, before any question of belief: a seed knowing which way is up, a newborn knowing how to feed.

notes.t: Qaddara is to fix an amount, a size, a limit, and the noun qadar comes from it. What the verse pairs with it is not compulsion but hidaya, being shown the way, a word the Qur'an also uses of animals and of a road.
Musa gives Pharaoh nearly this answer when asked who his Lord is: the One who gave each thing its creation and then guided it.
The exegetes read qaddara here at two widths: the general decree covering all things, and the narrower shaping of each creature to the work it does.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries both; the difference is one of scope rather than of substance

links.why: Musa's answer to Pharaoh, in almost these words
He created everything and determined it with a measure

4.sense: The third clause, and the subject drops from creation as such to grass. After the making of everything and the measuring of everything comes the specific fact that green fodder comes up out of the ground for animals to eat.

notes.t: Marʿa is pasture, what grazing animals eat, not crops grown for people. The surah reaches for the lowest end of the food chain and sets it beside the making of the heavens.
The Qur'an uses this same word for what the earth was made to yield, listing its water and its pasture together in An-Naziʿat.
Akhraja, brought out, treats the plant as something already held in the ground and then produced, which is the ordinary way the Qur'an describes growth.

links.why: the same word for pasture, in a list of what the earth yields
a longer list of what comes out of split ground, ending with fodder for the cattle

5.sense: The same pasture, one clause later. Ghutha is the wreckage a flood leaves stranded, froth and dead stalks caught on a bank. Ahwa is the colour something turns once it has dried and started to rot. The green is shown and then taken away inside the same sentence.

notes.t: The four clauses have moved from making, to measuring, to feeding, to withering. The last one is not a break in the list. It belongs to the same competence as the rest.

Ahwa is read either as the dark colour dead growth turns, or as a description of the pasture at its greenest, so deep a green that it is nearly black, in which case the ruin is carried by ghuthaʾ alone.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both and prefers the sense of darkened after drying

notes.t: The Qur'an uses the same arc as a picture of this life: growth that pleases the farmers, then a turn to yellow, then broken stubble.

links.why: growth and collapse used as a picture of this life
vegetation that becomes dry remnants scattered by the winds

6.sense: The address turns to the Prophet ﷺ and answers a worry he had not said out loud. The receiving of the Qur'an is being handled at the other end. He will be made to recite it, and the not forgetting follows from that rather than from his own effort.

notes.t: The verb is causative, We will cause you to recite. He is not being told to memorise harder. He is being told who is doing the work.
The Qur'an addresses the same anxiety directly elsewhere, telling him not to move his tongue with it to hurry it, because its gathering and its recitation are upon Us.
The sin at the front of the verb is a future marker. What is promised had not fully happened when it was said, which fits a revelation still arriving in pieces over years.

links.why: the same instruction given at length, with its reason
do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is finished

7.sense: An exception is attached to a promise that had just been stated flatly. Even the guarantee of memory stays under His will rather than being handed over. Then the reason is given, which is that nothing spoken and nothing concealed sits outside His knowledge.

notes.t: The exegetes differ on what the exception covers: verses Allah chose to withdraw, an exception stated to keep the matter under His will without anything in fact being forgotten, or the ordinary lapses of a human being.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record the several positions and the commentaries settle on none

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ heard a man reciting at night and said that the man had reminded him of a verse he had been made to drop from a certain surah, so the forgetting of a verse is reported of him and treated as something done to him rather than by him.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, from ʿAʾisha; also in Muslim

notes.t: Jahr is what is out in the open, said in a voice others hear. It is set against what is hidden, and the pair covers everything without listing anything.

links.why: whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better
He knows the secret and whatever is more hidden than it

words.g: and We will make you easy

8.sense: A second promise, and the wording is not the expected one. It does not say We will make the matter easy for you. It says We will make you easy for the easier way, which puts the smoothing on the man rather than on the road.

notes.t: Yusra is a superlative in the feminine, the easier or the easiest. Al-Layl sets it against ʿusra, hardship, and eases two different men toward two different ends using this same verb.
The Qur'an uses this root of the Book itself, saying more than once that We have made the Qur'an easy to remember, so is there anyone who will take it in.
The verse does not promise the absence of difficulty. It promises a fit between the man and the work he has been given.

links.why: the same verb twice, easing one man toward ease and another toward hardship
with hardship comes ease, said twice over

9.sense: The instruction that follows from the two promises. Remind. The condition hung on it has been argued over for as long as there has been commentary, because read flatly it appears to make reminding optional.

notes.t: The conditional is read three ways: as a real condition, so that effort goes where it may do some good; as meaning since the reminder benefits, which Arabic can do with in for a settled fact; and as addressed to the Prophet ﷺ's ﷺ own situation with people who had already refused.
notes.src: at-Tabari, az-Zamakhshari and ar-Razi each argue different sides of this

notes.t: The Qur'an tells the Prophet ﷺ plainly that he is a reminder and nothing further, not a controller set over people, which is the same limit placed on the same task.
Dhikra is a reminder, not new information. The Qur'an treats most of what it says as something people already knew and stopped attending to.

links.why: you are only a reminder, you are not over them a controller
remind, for the reminder benefits the believers

10.sense: Who the reminder lands on. Not whoever is clever, whoever has read more, or whoever was raised in it, but whoever has khashya, the fear that comes from some sense of who it is you are dealing with.

notes.t: Khashya is not fright. The lexicographers tie it to fear that grows out of knowing the thing feared, which is why the Qur'an says it is the people of knowledge among His servants who have it.
The Qur'an says a warning only reaches the one who follows the reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen, which names the same audience.
This verse quietly answers the condition put in the verse before it. The reminder does benefit, and here is the man it benefits.

links.why: it is those with knowledge among His servants who fear Him
the warning reaching the one who fears the Most Merciful unseen

words.g: and he keeps clear of it

11.sense: The other man, described by what he does with his body rather than with his argument. Yatajannab is to keep a thing off your side, to give it a wide berth. He does not dispute the reminder. He walks around it.

notes.t: The verb is built on janb, a side or a flank, so avoidance here is spatial, the way a man avoids a particular street. The picture is of a life arranged so that the reminder never comes up.

Ashqa is a superlative, the most wretched, and it is being said of a man who may be in the middle of what looks like a successful life. The word is a verdict on where he ends, not on how he currently appears.
The Qur'an uses this same superlative of the man who will enter the fire in Al-Layl, and of the one of Thamud who came forward to hamstring the camel.

links.why: none will enter it except the most wretched
the most wretched of Thamud, sent forward by his own people

12.sense: The wretched man is defined by what happens to him next rather than by anything he said. The fire is called the greatest, and calling it that implies smaller ones somewhere.

notes.t: Naming it the greatest fire raises the question of what the lesser one is. The suggestions offered include the fires of this world and the punishment of the grave. Neither is stated in the verse.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record the suggestions without treating any as decided

notes.t: Al-kubra is feminine because nar is feminine in Arabic. It is a superlative, the greatest, rather than an adjective meaning large.
The Qur'an uses this same verb of the fujjar in Al-Infitar, and in both places it means burning in contact rather than standing near heat.

links.why: the same verb of burning, said of the same kind of man
a fire named and the man warned that he will meet it

13.sense: The condition is described by removing both of the ways out. Death would end it. Living would let something be built on. Neither is available, and the line is short enough to close both exits before a reader has looked for a third.

notes.t: Both verbs are present tense in the Arabic, which describes a state going on rather than an event. It does not say he will not die. It says he does not die, continuously.
The Qur'an says elsewhere that death comes at such a man from every direction and yet he does not die, which is the same idea stated from the other side.
The verse is a definition of the worst case as the Qur'an frames it, which is not pain by itself but pain with no term attached and nothing growing out of it.

links.why: death coming at him from everywhere while he does not die
the same two denials, he neither dies in it nor lives

14.sense: The surah turns back to the other man and states his outcome in the past tense. Has succeeded, already, as a finished thing, said about somebody who is still alive and still working at it.

notes.t: Falah is a farmer's word before it is a religious one. The root means to split open and a fallah is a ploughman. Success in Arabic begins as the breaking of hard ground so that something can come up through it.
Tazakka is reflexive, he purified himself. The same root gives zakat, and it carries cleaning and growth at once, which is why a purified thing in Arabic is also an increased one.

Some early exegetes read tazakka here as paying zakat al-fitr and the next verse as the Eid prayer that follows it. Others keep the words general, since the surah is Meccan and zakat al-fitr was legislated in Madina.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the reports and prefers the general meaning

links.why: he has succeeded who purifies the soul, using both of this verse's words
the believers have succeeded, the same verb in the same finished tense

15.sense: Two more things about the same man, and the order is worth noticing. He remembered the name of his Lord, and then he prayed. The remembering comes first and the prayer comes out of it.

notes.t: The phrase the name of his Lord repeats the opening command of the surah almost word for word. The man who succeeded is the man who did what verse one told him to do.
The exegetes differ over whether salla here means the five daily prayers, the Eid prayer, or turning to Allah in prayer generally, and the Meccan setting of the surah bears on the answer.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir carry the several positions

notes.t: Three verbs describe the successful man across these two verses and not one of them is about what he believed. Purified, remembered, prayed. All three are things a bystander could watch him do.

links.why: the command this man is shown carrying out
establish the prayer for My remembrance, the same two joined

16.sense: The address swings round to a crowd and names what actually happens. Not you deny the next life, but you prefer this one, which is a statement about choosing between two things a person accepts are both there.

notes.t: Athara is to give a thing preference, and the noun ithar is the praised habit of preferring somebody else over yourself. The same verb is used here of preferring the nearer life over the later one.
Dunya is a comparative, the nearer, from the root of danaa, to be close. The Qur'an's ordinary name for this world is not the false life or the low life. It is the near one.
The same verb names the man whose refuge is the blaze: as for the one who transgressed and preferred the life of this world.

links.why: the same verb, preferring the nearer life, and what follows it
you love the fleeting one and leave the Hereafter, with the same bal

17.sense: The correction, made on the same terms the preference was made on. Two comparatives: better, and lasting longer. The verse does not tell anybody to stop wanting good things. It says the other option scores higher on both counts a person would actually use.

notes.t: Both words are comparatives, which concedes that this life has something in it. It is not being called worthless. It is being outbid.
The Qur'an repeats this exact pairing elsewhere, including of what is with Allah for those who believe and rely on their Lord.
Abqa comes from baqiya, to remain. The Qur'an's usual complaint against this life is its short term rather than its contents.

links.why: the last is better for you than the first
what is with Allah is better and longer lasting, do you not reason

18.sense: A claim about age. Whatever this refers to, it is not new and it was written down before. The surah has just said that the Hereafter is better and lasts longer, and now says that this was already in the oldest pages there are.

notes.t: What hadha points back to is disputed. Some exegetes take it as the two verses just before, the preferring of this life and the superiority of the next. Others take it as the whole surah, and others as the substance of the message in general.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir carry all three and the wording does not decide between them

notes.t: Suhuf are sheets or pages, the plural of sahifa. The word is not kitab, a bound book, and the Qur'an keeps it for revelation described as loose pages rather than as a codex.
The Qur'an uses this same word of the pages the angels carry and of the records spread open on the Day, so suhuf covers more than earlier scripture alone.

links.why: the pages of Musa and of Ibrahim who fulfilled what he was given
has the evidence of what is in the earlier pages not reached them

19.sense: The pages are named. Two prophets, one long before the other, and the surah ends by attaching what it has just said to both of them. Nothing of their contents is quoted here beyond what the verses above already said.

notes.t: The Qur'an names the pages of Ibrahim in only one other place, and both times it pairs them with the pages of Musa. Nothing of their text survives that Muslims are asked to hold to.

The other passage adds that Ibrahim fulfilled what he was given, and then lists what those pages carried: that no bearer of a burden bears the burden of another, and that a man has only what he worked for.
Ending on two earlier prophets does the same work as the surah's opening. The command to glorify the name of your Lord is presented as the oldest instruction there is rather than a new one.

links.why: the same two sets of pages, with a sample of what was written in them
we make no distinction between any of them, these two included

1.sense: The surah opens by pointing at a man. It does not define denial, it asks whether you have noticed a particular person. Everything after this is the answer, and the answer is given entirely in terms of what he does with his hands and his time.

notes.t: A-raʾayta in Arabic often carries the sense of tell me about, more than have you literally laid eyes on. Either way it puts a man in front of the listener before any doctrine is discussed.
Din here is the reckoning, the settling of an account, as in Master of the Day of Din. What is being described is a man who does not believe anything is being added up.
The exegetes name several men as the occasion for these verses, among them al-ʿAs ibn Waʾil and Abu Jahl. The reports are weak, they do not agree with each other, and the surah names nobody.
notes.src: the commentaries record several names with weak chains and no agreement between them

links.why: the same denial named in nearly the same words
those who deny the Day of Recompense, and what kind of man does it

2.sense: The evidence offered for a man's denial of the reckoning is not something he said. It is how he handles a child with nobody standing behind him. The fa at the front makes this verse the consequence of the one before it.

notes.t: Daʿʿa is a physical verb, to push somebody away roughly. The Qur'an uses it of the deniers being thrust toward the fire, so the man is doing now what will be done to him then.
The Qur'an uses this same verb of the Day itself, when they are shoved into the fire of Hell with a shove.
Belief in what cannot be seen is tested here against a visible act, and the person chosen for the test is the one least able to answer back. An orphan cannot retaliate and has nobody to complain to.

links.why: the same verb turned back on him on the Day
as for the orphan, do not treat him harshly

3.sense: The second charge is lighter than the first and worse for being lighter. He is not accused of refusing to feed the poor. He is accused of never urging anybody else to. The bar is set at speech and he does not clear it.

notes.t: Hadda is to push somebody toward doing a thing, to press them into it. The verse does not ask for his money. It asks whether he ever encouraged anyone else to part with theirs.
The Qur'an brings this same charge almost word for word against a man in Al-Haqqah, who did not believe in Allah the Great and did not urge the feeding of the destitute.
Miskin is not simply a poor man. The root is sukun, stillness, and the word describes somebody whom need has brought to a standstill.

links.why: the same charge, in a list of the reasons a man is in the fire
you do not honour the orphan nor urge the feeding of the poor, the same pair

4.sense: The surah turns and the sentence lands somewhere nobody was expecting. Woe to those who pray. Taken on its own the line is alarming, and it is meant to be held on its own for a moment before the next verse narrows it.

notes.t: Wayl is a word of ruin and lament. The verse attaches it to musallin, the people who pray, and leaves it attached for one whole verse.
In the Uthmani text this is a verse of its own and a reciter has to stop at the end of it. The pause is part of what the passage does to a listener.

The Qur'an keeps prayer and the treatment of the poor together in more than one place, describing those who pray and then describing what they set aside for the beggar, so the turn here is not a change of subject.

links.why: those who pray, described next by what they give the beggar
standing for prayer lazily and making a show of it to people

5.sense: The narrowing arrives. The preposition is an, away from, not fi, inside. The complaint is not about a mind wandering during prayer, which happens to everybody. It is about the prayer itself being the thing a man is careless with.

notes.t: Arabic distinguishes forgetfulness inside the prayer from neglect of the prayer as a whole, and the verse uses the second construction, which is why the early scholars did not read it as a condemnation of distraction.
A report from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas explains the verse as praying past the proper time. Whether it goes back to the Prophet ﷺ or is Saʿd's own reading of it is disputed by those who record it.
notes.src: narrated from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas by Abu Yaʿla and al-Bazzar; its status as a prophetic report is contested

notes.t: The order of the surah puts the man's handling of the orphan first and his prayer second, which is a way of saying which of the two gave him away.

links.why: and those who guard their prayers, said of the ones who succeed
prayer performed slackly and remembering Allah only a little

6.sense: The third description, and it explains the second. The prayer is not neglected because the man is lazy. It is neglected because it was never addressed to the One it names. It was addressed to whoever was watching.

notes.t: Yuraʾun is a reciprocal form of the verb to see, meaning to show and be seen at once. The man performs and the audience hands him what he came for.
The Qur'an describes the hypocrites in these terms, standing for prayer lazily, making a show of it to people and remembering Allah only a little.

A report has the Prophet ﷺ say that what he feared most for his people was the lesser association, and when asked what that was, he answered riyaʾ, showing off. It is in Ahmad and a number of scholars grade it acceptable.
notes.src: Ahmad, from Mahmud ibn Labid; graded hasan by several scholars and questioned by others

links.why: charity cancelled by a man who spends to be seen by people
do not be like those who went out showing off to people

7.sense: The surah ends on the smallest item in it. Not wealth and not charity, but maʿun, and the closing charge against a man who denies the reckoning is that he will not lend out a bucket.

notes.t: What maʿun means is one of the oldest disagreements in exegesis. Ibn Masʿud is reported to have said it is the things people lend one another, a pot, an axe, a bucket. Reports from Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAli read it as zakat.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects both lines of report and the commentaries have never settled on one

notes.t: If maʿun is household lending, the surah has walked down from denying the Day, through shoving an orphan, to refusing a neighbour a cooking pot, and its point is that one man does all of it.

The last word of the surah is its name. A reader who wants to know what religion looks like once it has been emptied out is given seven verses, and the final item on the list is the least costly thing on it.

links.why: those who are miserly and instruct other people in miserliness
when good touches him he holds it back, the same root
